title: the quiet the mystics share
hookLine: mystics disagree about almost everything; they all got quiet
tomorrow: the Tao: those who know they have enough are rich

lines: WHEN DID YOU LAST HEAR NOTHING?
cards: When was the last time you heard nothing? Not quiet with a podcast. Not quiet with the fridge humming and a phone buzzing in the next room.
Nothing. It's easy to go a long time without it. The car, the shower, the walk to the store all get filled.
Here's something odd. The mystics of the world's traditions disagree about a great deal: God, the soul, what happens after death.
But read what they actually did, and one thing keeps showing up, from monasteries to meeting houses to mountain caves. They got quiet.

teach.h: NOT THE WIND, NOT THE FIRE.
teach.b: Start with a prophet on the run. Elijah hides in a cave on a mountain. A great wind comes, tearing rocks apart, but God is not in the wind.
Then an earthquake, and God is not in the earthquake. Then fire, and God is not in the fire. And then, in the King James wording, "after the fire a still small voice."
That Hebrew phrase is hard to carry into English; it has also been rendered a gentle whisper, and a sound of thin silence. Either way, what comes after the noise is quiet.
Eastern Orthodox monks on Mount Athos in Greece are known for a way of prayer called hesychasm, from a Greek word meaning stillness.
In traditional Quaker meetings, Friends worship by sitting together in silence, speaking only when someone feels moved to.
Early Buddhist texts describe the Buddha telling monks that when they gather, they should either talk about the teaching or keep what he called noble silence.
And an old Chinese classic puts it sharply: those who know don't talk about it, and those who talk about it don't know. These traditions don't agree about what's found in the silence.
For some it's God; for some, the mind seeing itself clearly; for some, the Tao, which can't be named.
But it's a room each of them walks into. For each, in its own way, quiet is where it is.

how: Silence is practiced in many forms: Quaker meetings for worship held in shared silence, silent retreats in Christian and Buddhist monasteries, and the Orthodox practice of stillness called hesychasm.

games.q: who kept the silence — tap the pairs.
p: a still small voice after the fire
talk of the teaching, or noble silence

s: all mystics agree on what is found in the silence
they don't: God, a clear mind, the unnamed Tao. they share the room, not the answer.
in the Elijah story, God was not in the wind, the earthquake or the fire
Quaker worship is traditionally led by a preacher from a pulpit
in traditional Quaker meetings, people sit in silence and speak only when moved to.

games.q: you're Elijah in the cave. a wind splits the rocks, an earthquake shakes the mountain, a fire passes. where does the text say God was?
o: in none of them. then came a still small voice.
games.why: not in the wind, the earthquake or the fire. "after the fire a still small voice." what comes after the noise is quiet.

practice: Here's the practice. If you can, turn off one sound near you: the music, the TV, the notifications. Then sit.
For the next forty-five seconds, don't try to make the mind silent. Just listen to the silence that's already around the sounds. The hum, and the space around the hum.
If you pray, you can hold a line from the Psalms: be still, and know. If you don't, just listen.

wordCard.voice: Silence. A room that prophets, monks, Friends and sages all walk into, even when they find different things there. Twelfth word.

orig.note: Greek, hesychia: stillness, quiet. Eastern Orthodox Christians named a whole way of prayer after it, hesychasm.

carryVoice: Your line: quiet is where it is. A stretch you don't fill can be a room of its own. That's day twelve.
